transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

Ever since that robbery, I keep organizing my whole life around avoiding anything that reminds me of it—certain neighborhoods, late meetings, even some community events. I realized I've been arranging my entire life around just trying to feel safe, and a close friend suggested I finally come in to talk to someone.
Can you tell me more about what specifically happens when you're in a situation or place that reminds you of the robbery, how do you feel and what do you do?

To avoid reminders, I only schedule client visits in the morning and completely stay away from that part of town after dark. If I am triggered, like when locking up an office, I suddenly see myself back on that floor with the gun at my head, my chest tightens, and I can't catch my breath. I also feel incredibly anxious in those moments, constantly scanning for exits and jumping out of my skin at any sudden noise.
Do you experience excessive and persistent worry about everyday things, not just situations related to the robbery, and find it difficult to control this worry?

No, my worries are almost entirely focused on my safety and things that remind me of the robbery. I don't really experience uncontrollable worry about other normal, everyday matters. It's really just about trying to keep myself safe and avoiding those triggers.

Can you estimate how much of your daily life or activities have been affected by these avoidance behaviors and flashbacks, would you say it's significantly impacted your social, work, or personal relationships?

It has had a massive impact, and I feel like my whole world has shrunk. Over the past year, I've turned down promotions, evening speaking gigs, and pulled back from my mentoring and church activities. It's gotten to the point where my friends and coworkers have started asking why I'm not showing up like I used to.
Can you tell me if you've experienced any difficulty recalling specific details of the robbery, or if there are parts of that event that you can't remember at all?

Yes, there are definitely blank spots from that night that I just can't recall. While I vividly remember lying on the floor and hearing the young employee crying, other parts—like what the robber actually said to me or how long it all lasted—are completely blank no matter how hard I try to piece it together.
Do you ever feel as though you're observing yourself from outside your body or as if you're in a dream during these flashbacks or when confronted with reminders of the robbery?

No, I don't feel like I'm outside of my body or in a dream at all. Instead, I feel very much trapped in my own body, with my chest tightening up, my heart racing, and feeling an intense, overwhelming fear.
Have you experienced any feelings of detachment from others or the world around you, as if people or things seem unreal or distant, especially when not having a flashback?

Yes, I absolutely feel that way, like I'm watching everyone from behind glass even when I'm at church or a family barbecue. I nod and smile in the right places, but I feel completely disconnected and like I'm not really part of it. It just feels like nobody truly understands what I'm going through anymore.
Do you also experience significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning due to these feelings of detachment or avoidance behaviors?

Yes, it has severely impacted my life across the board. I've turned down promotions, evening speaking engagements, and downtown events, and I've pulled back from mentoring and church activities. It's gotten to the point where my friends and coworkers are constantly asking why I'm not showing up like I used to.

Can you tell me if you've experienced any persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about yourself, others, or the world, such as feeling guilty for surviving the robbery or believing that the world is completely unsafe?

Yes, I struggle with those thoughts constantly. I often blame myself, thinking I was stupid to be at the store so late and should have known better. I also feel like the world has become an ugly and dangerous place, and I can never truly let my guard down anymore.

Can you describe how your negative beliefs about yourself and the world, such as feeling guilty for surviving the robbery or believing the world is completely unsafe, contribute to your avoidance behaviors and overall distress?

Because I constantly blame myself for being 'stupid' enough to be at the store so late, I feel like I can't trust my own judgment. Since I now believe the world is just too dangerous and I can never let my guard down, I avoid evening events, downtown areas, and late meetings to keep myself from feeling that intense dread. It's just easier to stay away than to risk feeling that terror again.
